header_evidence.explanation: The document opens with the title 'LIT-IN-ENGLISH' (occurs once) and then this scheme heading, which occurs once and names Literature-in-English and class SS1; the document has no 'SUBJECT:' line. The subject is verified by the document and not by the filename, and it is not English Language: the scheme lists introduction to the study of literature, genres (drama, prose, poetry), fiction and non-fiction, elements of prose, features and forms of poetry, drama, oral literature, and Week 1 teaching separates English Literature from Literature-In-English. The heading differs from the canonical name by the 'SCHEME OF WORK FOR' prefix and class label, so a source_alias is declared.

It names Literature-in-English, and lines 1 and 3 name the second term and class SS1, so subject and term are verified by the document and not by the filename. The scheme lists African drama (Harvest of Corruption, The Blood of a Stranger), African poetry (Piano and Drums) and further set texts, and Week One teaches Harvest of Corruption, so it is not English Language. The heading differs from the canonical name 'Literature-in-English' (used by LIT-SRC-T1) by spaces and en dashes, so a source_alias is declared. The scheme lists African drama (Harvest of Corruption, The Blood of a Stranger), African poetry (Piano and Drums, The Dining Table, The Anvil and the Hammer) and non-African drama (Othello, She Stoops to Conquer), and Week One teaches Harvest of Corruption, so it is not English Language. evidence.explanation: The paragraph states the distinction in two sentences and gives no example, no work or author for the second term, and no reason the two are separated. Two claims are checkable and unreferenced: (a) the Beowulf date range and 'national epic' status; (b) the scope claim for Literature In English. 'despite being Scandinavia' is garbled (the poem's setting is Scandinavia; the sentence does not say so). Checked on 2026-11-07 through web copies only, not a page-cited edition: an Oxford Old English course page dates the Beowulf manuscript to around the turn of the eleventh century, gives no single composition date and says the competing composition-date theories lack consensus; the WASSCE Literature-in-English syllabus (a web copy) divides its texts into African and non-African prose, drama and poetry and never frames the subject as works from British colonies. The distinction as taught is therefore not settled and is recorded as a FACT open item. Not retaught here.
